title: Optic Atrophy: Optic Neuritis, Optic Neuropathies and Papilledema

questions.sec: Optic atrophy — clinical features and the Rostenbaum index
questions.q: Per the book, the state of the optic disc is representative of the:
questions.exp: Optic atrophy: conditions of the optic disc are representative of the optic nerve. (Book p32)

questions.sec: Optic atrophy — clinical features and the Rostenbaum index
questions.q: The first classical sign of optic atrophy in the book is:
opts: Enlargement of the optic cup with a deep excavation
Pallor of the optic disc d/t loss of vascularity
questions.exp: Clinical feature 1: pallor of the OD (d/t loss of vascularity) — the first classical sign. (Book p32)

questions.sec: Optic atrophy — clinical features and the Rostenbaum index
questions.q: Fill up: the loss of vascularity in optic atrophy is quantified by the ______ index, the ratio of small to large blood vessels.
questions.exp: Loss of vascularity is defined by the Rostenbaum index — ratio of small : large blood vessels. (Book p32)

questions.sec: Optic atrophy — clinical features and the Rostenbaum index
questions.q: Per the book, the Rostenbaum index in a normal disc is greater than ______, and in optic atrophy it is less than ______.
questions.exp: Normal ratio >10; optic atrophy <7, reflecting loss of small vessels on the OD. (Book p32)

questions.sec: Optic atrophy — clinical features and the Rostenbaum index
questions.q: A patient with optic atrophy on fundus review still reads 6/6. The book explains this is possible because:
opts: The affected fibres determine the field loss; central fibres may be spared
The optic cup is filled up d/t swelling
questions.exp: Visual field loss depends on the affected fibres; a patient may have 6/6 vision if central fibres are spared. (Book p32)

questions.sec: Optic atrophy — clinical features and the Rostenbaum index
questions.q: All of the following are labelled on the book's normal optic disc photograph EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Normal OD photograph: optic cup (yellowish) and pink/orange neuroretinal ring; waxy pallor belongs to consecutive (retinal) atrophy. (Book p32)

questions.sec: Types of optic atrophy — primary, secondary and consecutive
questions.q: Match the atrophy type with its definition — 1) Primary (1°) 2) Secondary (2°) 3) Consecutive … A) D/t disease of the inner retina and its blood supply B) Atrophy after optic disc swelling C) Atrophy without antecedent optic disc swelling
questions.exp: Primary (1°): atrophy without antecedent disc swelling; Secondary (2°): atrophy after disc swelling; Consecutive: d/t disease of the inner retina and its blood supply. (Book p33)

questions.sec: Types of optic atrophy — primary, secondary and consecutive
questions.q: Match the atrophy type with the disc appearance in the book's table — 1) Primary 2) Secondary 3) Consecutive … A) Waxy pallor of the disc, less sharply defined margins B) Dirty gray-white, ill-defined margins C) Chalky white, well defined margins
questions.exp: Primary: chalky white, well defined margins; Secondary: dirty gray-white, ill-defined margins; Consecutive: waxy pallor, less sharply defined margins. (Book p33)

questions.sec: Types of optic atrophy — primary, secondary and consecutive
questions.q: All of the following are listed causes of primary optic atrophy EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Primary causes: optic neuritis (m/c cause multiple sclerosis), tumors, trauma, hereditary, toxic; papilledema is a cause of secondary atrophy. (Book p33)

questions.sec: Types of optic atrophy — primary, secondary and consecutive
questions.q: In the book's table, the vessels in secondary atrophy show:
questions.exp: Vessels: primary — normal; secondary — peripapillary sheathing; consecutive — attenuation. (Book p33)

questions.sec: Types of optic atrophy — primary, secondary and consecutive
questions.q: Which statement about the optic cup in atrophy types is FALSE per the book?
questions.exp: Optic cup: primary — shallow, saucer shaped; secondary — filled up d/t swelling; consecutive — normal. (Book p33)

questions.sec: Types of optic atrophy — primary, secondary and consecutive
questions.q: All of the following are listed retinal diseases producing consecutive atrophy EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Consecutive (retinal) causes: retinitis seen CRAO/CRVO, healed vasculitis, panretinal photo-coagulation, retinitis pigmentosa; optic neuritis is a primary cause. (Book p33)

questions.sec: Types of optic atrophy — primary, secondary and consecutive
questions.q: Fill up: the surrounding retina in secondary atrophy shows ______.
questions.exp: Surrounding retina: primary — normal; secondary — hyaline bodies/drusen; consecutive — pathology seen. (Book p33)

questions.sec: Optic neuritis — types and the macular star
questions.q: Match the optic neuritis type with its part of the nerve and key feature — 1) Papillitis 2) Retrobulbar neuritis 3) Neuroretinitis (papillitis + maculitis) … A) M/c in adults, no visible sign, associated with MS B) M/c in children, disc hyperemia, flame shaped haemorrhages C) Macular star appearance, associated with viral infections
questions.exp: Papillitis (intraocular part), m/c in children: disc hyperemia, flame shaped haemorrhages in/around the disc. Retrobulbar (intraorbital/intracanalicular/intracranial), m/c in adults: no visible sign, loss of vision, MS association. Neuroretinitis: macular star, viral associations. (Book p34)

questions.sec: Optic neuritis — types and the macular star
questions.q: Fill up: in neuroretinitis the macular star appearance is produced by exudates radiating from the ______.
questions.exp: Neuroretinitis photograph: papillitis with macular star appearance d/t exudates radiating from the macula. (Book p34)

questions.sec: Optic neuritis — types and the macular star
questions.q: The book's mnemonic NHAP lists causes of the macular star. All of the following belong EXCEPT:
questions.exp: NHAP: Neuroretinitis, Hypertensive retinopathy, Angioma (retinal), Papilledema; CRAO is not in the mnemonic. (Book p34)

questions.sec: Optic neuritis — types and the macular star
questions.q: The book's mnemonic 'a CuP mar' lists clinical features of optic neuritis d/t multiple sclerosis. All of the following belong EXCEPT:
questions.exp: MS features: central scotoma, colour blindness (red ↓ green), unilateral (m/c) loss of vision, Uhthoff's phenomenon; Horner's syndrome is not listed. (Book p34)

questions.sec: Optic neuritis — types and the macular star
questions.q: Uhthoff's phenomenon, listed with MS-related optic neuritis, is:
opts: Improvement of vision with a rise in body temperature
Worsening of symptoms with a rise in body temperature (e.g. during exercise)
Transitory complete blindness during sleep only
Pain that eases with ocular movement, worsens at rest
questions.exp: Uhthoff's phenomenon: ↑ body temperature (eg: during exercise) → worsening of symptoms. (Book p34)

questions.sec: Optic neuritis — MS features, pain and the earliest sign
questions.q: The Pulfrich phenomenon in optic neuritis is:
opts: An altitudinal defect respecting the horizontal midline
Colour blindness for red and green
Altered perception of kinetic (fast moving) objects with static objects normal
questions.exp: Pulfrich phenomenon: altered perception of kinetic objects (static → normal) d/t optic nerve demyelination → ↓ speed of impulse conduction → inaccurate perception of fast moving objects. (Book p35)

questions.sec: Optic neuritis — MS features, pain and the earliest sign
questions.q: A 26-year-old woman with acute optic neuritis reports pain that worsens whenever she moves her eyes. Per the book the mechanism is:
opts: Ciliary spasm from the near reflex
Corneal nerve involvement with surface pain
Extraocular muscle inflammation through the common sheath
questions.exp: Pain in the eye: exaggerated with ocular movements — ON inflammation → extraocular muscle inflammation (d/t common sheath) → muscles inflamed → pain on movement. (Book p35)

questions.sec: Optic neuritis — MS features, pain and the earliest sign
questions.q: The earliest sign of optic neuritis per the book is:
questions.exp: Marcus Gunn pupil/RAPD: earliest sign of optic neuritis. (Book p35)

questions.sec: Optic neuritis — ONTT, beta-IFN and glatiramer
questions.q: Per the ONTT protocol, the treatment regimen for a qualifying optic neuritis patient is:
opts: Oral prednisone 1 mg/kg/day for 11 days alone
IV methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 3 days → oral prednisone 1 mg/kg/day for 11 days
IV methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 11 days only
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day for 3 days → IV for 11 days
questions.exp: ONTT: steroids — IV methylprednisolone 1g/day × 3 days → oral prednisone 1mg/kg/day × 11 days; exclusive oral steroids are C/I due to ↑ chances of relapse. (Book p35)

questions.sec: Optic neuritis — ONTT, beta-IFN and glatiramer
questions.q: Which statement about the ONTT is FALSE per the book?
opts: Eligibility requires vision at initial presentation <6/12
Eligibility requires no previous episode of multiple sclerosis and/or optic neuritis
Eligibility requires ≥1 demyelinating lesion on MRI
questions.exp: ONTT criteria: vision at presentation <6/12; no previous episode of MS and/or optic neuritis; ≥1 demyelinating lesion on MRI; exclusive oral steroids are C/I (↑ relapse). (Book p35)

questions.sec: Optic neuritis — ONTT, beta-IFN and glatiramer
questions.q: Fill up: the ONTT showed that steroids hasten recovery but produce ______ in the final visual outcome.
opts: A permanent gain of one line
questions.exp: ONTT outcome: hastens recovery; no change in visual outcome. (Book p35)

questions.sec: Optic neuritis — ONTT, beta-IFN and glatiramer
questions.q: Match the agent with its role in the book's treatment list — 1) Post-steroidal β-IFN 2) Glatiramer acetate 3) Exclusive oral steroids … A) 20 mg s/c injection B) C/I — ↑ chances of relapse C) CHAMPS study: good outcome → ↓ MS occurrence
questions.exp: Post-steroidal β-IFN (CHAMPS study: good outcome → ↓ occurrence of MS in optic neuritis patients); glatiramer acetate 20 mg s/c; exclusive oral steroids C/I. (Book p35)

questions.sec: Neuromyelitis optica (Devic's) and hereditary optic neuropathies
questions.q: The pathology of neuromyelitis optica (Devic's disease) per the book is:
questions.exp: NMO/Devic's: demyelinating disease, m/c in young females; cause — can be 2° to multiple sclerosis; pathology d/t aquaporin 4 (AQP-4 autoantigen). (Book p35)

questions.sec: Neuromyelitis optica (Devic's) and hereditary optic neuropathies
questions.q: All of the following are listed presentation features of neuromyelitis optica EXCEPT:
opts: ↑ chance of relapse (more than in multiple sclerosis alone)
questions.exp: Presentation: B/L optic neuritis + transverse myelitis; ↑ chance of relapse (more than in MS alone). Ptosis is not listed. (Book p35)

questions.sec: Neuromyelitis optica (Devic's) and hereditary optic neuropathies
questions.q: Match the hereditary optic neuropathy with its genetics in the book's table — 1) Kjer/dominant optic atrophy 2) Behr 3) Wolfram (DIDMOAD) … A) Autosomal recessive with ataxia, nystagmus, mental retardation B) Autosomal dominant C) Autosomal recessive with DI, DM, deafness
questions.exp: Kjer/dominant optic atrophy — autosomal dominant (no remarks); Behr — autosomal recessive (ataxia, nystagmus, mental retardation); Wolfram/DIDMOAD (DI, DM, optic atrophy, deafness) — autosomal recessive (associations DI, DM, deafness). (Book p36)

questions.sec: Neuromyelitis optica (Devic's) and hereditary optic neuropathies
questions.q: Per the book, Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) carries a point mutation at codon ______.
questions.exp: LHON: mitochondrial inheritance (maternally transmitted, m > F); point mutation at codon 11778. (Book p36)

questions.sec: Neuromyelitis optica (Devic's) and hereditary optic neuropathies
questions.q: A 24-year-old man presents with painless B/L loss of vision, dilated tortuous peripapillary vessels and pseudo-papillitis. Per the book the diagnosis, and its pathognomonic feature, is:
questions.exp: LHON features: presents in 2nd/3rd decade, painless loss (B/L > U/L), pupillary telangiectasia, pseudo-papillitis, 1° optic atrophy, central scotoma; injury to fibres between disc and macula — papillomacular degeneration is the pathognomonic feature; no treatment so far. (Book p36)

questions.sec: Neuromyelitis optica (Devic's) and hereditary optic neuropathies
questions.q: For neuromyelitis optica the book lists which investigations and management?
opts: VEP alone, with glatiramer acetate as the treatment
Tonography first, then miotics as the treatment
NMO IgG (anti-AQP-4) antibodies, lumbar puncture, steroids for control
OCT alone, with no treatment planned
questions.exp: Investigations: measure NMO IgG antibodies (anti AQP-4 antibodies); lumbar puncture. Management: disease control with steroids. (Book p36)

questions.sec: Disc swelling differentials, toxic/nutritional neuropathy, papilledema character
questions.q: Which statement is FALSE per the book's note on mitochondrial and disc swelling entities?
opts: Mitochondrial diseases do not generally have a gender predilection
LHON is a cause of pseudo-papilledema
Optic disc drusen cause true papilledema
questions.exp: Note: mitochondrial diseases do not generally have a gender predilection. Disc swelling causes: ↑ ICP → papilledema; other (pseudo-papilledema) causes: LHON, methanol poisoning, near vision loss in hypermetropia, optic disc drusen, peripapillary myelinated nerve fibres. (Book p37)

questions.sec: Disc swelling differentials, toxic/nutritional neuropathy, papilledema character
questions.q: The book's DICE mnemonic lists ophthotoxic drugs. All of the following belong EXCEPT:
questions.exp: DICE: Digoxin, Isoniazid, Chloroquine, Ethambutol (most ophthotoxic drug). Sildenafil is listed under acquired colour blindness, not DICE. (Book p37)

questions.sec: Disc swelling differentials, toxic/nutritional neuropathy, papilledema character
questions.q: Per the book, the most ophthotoxic drug in the DICE mnemonic is:
questions.exp: Ethambutol is highlighted as the most ophthotoxic drug. (Book p37)

questions.sec: Disc swelling differentials, toxic/nutritional neuropathy, papilledema character
questions.q: For nutritional (tobacco–alcohol) optic amblyopia the book's Rx is:
questions.exp: Rx: hydroxocobalamin 1000 units weekly for 10 weeks. (Book p37)

questions.sec: Disc swelling differentials, toxic/nutritional neuropathy, papilledema character
questions.q: Fill up: along with vitamins B1 and B6, the book lists deficiency of vitamin ______ as a cause of toxic/nutritional optic neuropathy.
questions.exp: Causes of toxic/nutritional optic neuropathy: drugs (DICE), deficiency of vitamins B1/B6/B12, methanol poisoning. (Book p37)

questions.sec: Disc swelling differentials, toxic/nutritional neuropathy, papilledema character
questions.q: A 55-year-old heavy smoker and drinker presents with painless progressive visual loss and a central scotoma on perimetry. Per the book the entity and the field pattern are:
opts: Tobacco–alcohol amblyopia with a central (cecocentral) scotoma
Papilledema with an enlarged blind spot
Retrobulbar neuritis with a junctional scotoma
questions.exp: Toxic/nutritional optic neuropathy (tobacco–alcohol amblyopia) gives the central/cecocentral scotoma shown between the fovea and optic disc in the book's diagrams. (Book p37)

questions.sec: Disc swelling differentials, toxic/nutritional neuropathy, papilledema character
questions.q: The character of papilledema swelling per the book is:
questions.exp: Papilledema: swelling of the optic disc due to raised ICP; character — non-inflammatory (d/t hydrostatic pressure, passive), painless, B/L (except in Foster Kennedy syndrome). (Book p37)

questions.sec: Papilledema — pathogenesis, stages, ICP symptoms, Frisen grading; AION
questions.q: Match the papilledema pathogenesis step with its next event in the book's flowchart — 1) Raised ICP 2) Blockage of anterograde flow/axoplasmic transport 3) Venous congestion … A) Vascular signs B) Stasis in the optic disc C) Pressure transmitted along the subarachnoid space
questions.exp: Flowchart: raised ICP → pressure transmitted along subarachnoid space → pressure on optic nerve → blockage of anterograde flow/axoplasmic transport → stasis in optic disc → extracellular edema (mechanical signs) and venous congestion (vascular signs). (Book p38)

questions.sec: Papilledema — pathogenesis, stages, ICP symptoms, Frisen grading; AION
questions.q: Fill up: the earliest fundal sign of acute papilledema in the book is ______.
questions.exp: Acute papilledema: blurring of disc margins (earlier), elevated OD, Paton's lines; also hyperemia/congestion of the OD, loss of venous pulsations, hemorrhages around the OD. (Book p38)

questions.sec: Papilledema — pathogenesis, stages, ICP symptoms, Frisen grading; AION
questions.q: Paton's lines in the book are:
opts: Flame shaped hemorrhages on the disc
questions.exp: Paton's lines: retinochoroidal folds around the OD (d/t leakage of fluid). (Book p38)

questions.sec: Papilledema — pathogenesis, stages, ICP symptoms, Frisen grading; AION
questions.q: The chronic papilledema fundal appearance per the book is:
opts: Pink disc with a macular star
questions.exp: Chronic papilledema: champagne-cork appearance of the OD. (Book p38)

questions.sec: Papilledema — pathogenesis, stages, ICP symptoms, Frisen grading; AION
questions.q: Per the book, a swollen disc from the retrobulbar ON produces which visual field defect?
questions.exp: Retrobulbar ON → OD swollen → VFD: enlargement of the blind spot. (Book p38)

questions.sec: Papilledema — pathogenesis, stages, ICP symptoms, Frisen grading; AION
questions.q: A 45-year-old with a brain tumor has headaches that are worst in the morning, projectile vomiting, B/L disc swelling, and intact vision and light reflexes. Per the book the earliest sign of raised ICP is:
questions.exp: Symptoms of ICP: headache is the earliest sign, ↑ in morning, projectile vomiting, progressively worsens. (Book p38)

questions.sec: Papilledema — pathogenesis, stages, ICP symptoms, Frisen grading; AION
questions.q: Which statement about the ICP symptoms in the book is FALSE?
opts: Papilledema causes sudden painful LOV early in the course
Horizontal diplopia can occur d/t associated CN VI palsy
Amaurosis fugax episodes are diagnostic of stroke
Papilledema initially has no LOV and a normal pupillary light reflex
questions.exp: Papilledema: no LOV, normal pupillary light reflex, leads to 2° optic atrophy (gradual painless loss of vision); horizontal diplopia d/t associated CN VI palsy; amaurosis fugax — d/t brief cessation of axoplasmic transport: transient complete LOV, 30-60s episodes, total (6/6) recovery post attack, diagnostic of stroke. (Book p38)

questions.sec: Papilledema — pathogenesis, stages, ICP symptoms, Frisen grading; AION
questions.q: Per the book, each amaurosis fugax episode of papilledema lasts:
questions.exp: Amaurosis fugax: transient, complete LOV; 30-60s episodes; total (6/6) recovery of vision post attack. (Book p38)

questions.sec: Papilledema — pathogenesis, stages, ICP symptoms, Frisen grading; AION
questions.q: Match the Frisen grade of papilledema with its finding — 1) Grade 1 2) Grade 3 3) Grade 5 … A) All vessels obscured, ↑↑ venous engorgement → congestion B) 'C' shaped halo (swelling) of the OD C) Loss of major blood vessels around the disc
questions.exp: Frisen's grading: Grade 1 — 'C' shaped halo (swelling) in OD; Grade 2 — circumferential halo, blurred margins; Grade 3 — loss of major blood vessels around the disc; Grade 4 — loss of blood vessels on disc, ↑↑ swelling over disc; Grade 5 — all vessels obscured, ↑↑ venous engorgement → congestion. (Book p39)

questions.sec: Papilledema — pathogenesis, stages, ICP symptoms, Frisen grading; AION
questions.q: Which statement about anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (AION) is FALSE per the book?
opts: Arteritic AION is caused by giant cell arteritis (large vessel arteritis)
Non-arteritic AION (no vasculitis) follows occlusion of the short posterior ciliary artery
Both types give altitudinal field defects
Arteritic AION presents painlessly with U/L moderate visual loss
questions.exp: Arteritic AION: giant cell arteritis, temporal artery pathology, premonitory symptoms (pain, amaurosis fugax), B/L severe visual loss, treatment corticosteroids. Non-arteritic: occlusion of short posterior ciliary artery; associations — hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, collagen vascular diseases; painless, U/L moderate visual loss; experimental Rx levodopa + carbidopa for 3 weeks; both give altitudinal defects. (Book p39)

units.title: Optic atrophy — clinical features and the Rostenbaum index
units.guide: Conditions of the optic disc are representative of the optic nerve. Clinical features: (1) pallor of the OD d/t loss of vascularity — first classical sign; (2) loss of vascularity defined by the Rostenbaum index (ratio of small : large blood vessels) — normal >10, optic atrophy <7 (loss of small vessels on the OD); (3) visual field loss depends on the affected fibres — a patient may have 6/6 vision if central fibres are spared. Normal disc photograph: yellowish optic cup and pink/orange neuroretinal ring; atrophic disc: pale OD with reduced small vessels.

units.title: Types of optic atrophy — primary, secondary and consecutive
units.guide: Primary (1°): atrophy without antecedent disc swelling — chalky white, well defined margins; shallow saucer-shaped cup; normal vessels; normal surrounding retina; causes: optic neuritis (m/c cause multiple sclerosis), tumors, trauma, hereditary, toxic. Secondary (2°): atrophy after disc swelling — dirty gray-white, ill-defined margins; cup filled up d/t swelling; peripapillary sheathing; hyaline bodies/drusen; causes: papilledema, papillitis, AION. Consecutive: atrophy d/t disease of the inner retina and its blood supply — waxy pallor, less sharply defined margins; normal cup; vessel attenuation; pathology seen; retinal diseases: retinitis seen CRAO/CRVO, healed vasculitis, panretinal photo-coagulation, retinitis pigmentosa.

units.title: Optic neuritis — types, the macular star and MS features
units.guide: Optic neuritis = inflammation of the ON, an important cause of 1° atrophy. Parts of the ON: intraocular, intraorbital, intracanalicular, intracranial. Types: papillitis (intraocular) m/c in children — disc hyperemia, flame shaped haemorrhages in/around the disc; retrobulbar neuritis m/c in adults — no visible sign, loss of vision, associated with MS; neuroretinitis (papillitis + maculitis) — macular star appearance (exudates radiating from the macula), associated with viral infections. Macular star causes (NHAP): Neuroretinitis, Hypertensive retinopathy, Angioma (retinal), Papilledema. MS features (mnemonic a CuP mar): central scotoma, colour blindness (red ↓ green), unilateral (m/c) loss of vision, Uhthoff's phenomenon (↑ body temperature, e.g. during exercise → worsening of symptoms).

units.title: Optic neuritis — Pulfrich, pain, RAPD and the ONTT treatment
units.guide: Pulfrich phenomenon: altered perception of kinetic objects (static → normal) d/t ON demyelination → ↓ speed of impulse conduction → inaccurate perception of fast moving objects. Pain in the eye is exaggerated with ocular movements (ON inflammation → extraocular muscle inflammation d/t common sheath → pain on movement). Marcus Gunn pupil/RAPD: earliest sign. Treatment (ONTT): steroids — IV methylprednisolone 1g/day × 3 days → oral prednisone 1mg/kg/day × 11 days; exclusive oral steroids C/I (↑ relapse). Criteria: vision at presentation <6/12; no previous episode of MS and/or optic neuritis; ≥1 demyelinating lesion on MRI. Outcome: hastens recovery, no change in visual outcome. Post-steroidal β-IFN (CHAMPS study): good outcome → ↓ MS occurrence. Glatiramer acetate 20 mg s/c. NMO/Devic's: demyelinating, m/c in young females, can be 2° to MS; pathology d/t aquaporin 4 (AQP-4 autoantigen); presentation B/L optic neuritis + transverse myelitis, ↑ relapse than MS alone.

units.title: Devic's workup, hereditary optic neuropathies and toxic/nutritional neuropathy
units.guide: NMO investigations: NMO IgG (anti AQP-4) antibodies, lumbar puncture; management: disease control with steroids. Hereditary optic neuropathies: Kjer/dominant optic atrophy — autosomal dominant; Behr — autosomal recessive (ataxia, nystagmus, mental retardation); Wolfram/DIDMOAD (DI, DM, optic atrophy, deafness) — autosomal recessive (DI, DM, deafness); Leber's (LHON) — mitochondrial (maternal, m > F), point mutation at codon 11778, presents in 2nd/3rd decade, painless loss B/L > U/L, pupillary telangiectasia, pseudo-papillitis, 1° atrophy, central scotoma, papillomacular degeneration (pathognomonic), no treatment so far. Note: mitochondrial diseases do not generally have a gender predilection. Disc swelling causes: ↑ ICP → papilledema; pseudo-papilledema — LHON, methanol poisoning, near vision loss in hypermetropia, optic disc drusen, peripapillary myelinated nerve fibres. Toxic/nutritional (tobacco–alcohol amblyopia): drugs DICE (Digoxin, Isoniazid, Chloroquine, Ethambutol — most ophthotoxic), B1/B6/B12 deficiency, methanol poisoning; cecocentral scotoma; Rx hydroxocobalamin 1000 units weekly × 10 weeks. Papilledema: swelling of the OD d/t raised ICP — non-inflammatory (passive, hydrostatic), painless, B/L (except Foster Kennedy).

units.title: Papilledema — pathogenesis, stages, ICP symptoms, Frisen grading and AION
units.guide: Etiopathogenesis: raised ICP → pressure transmitted along subarachnoid space → pressure on the ON → blockage of anterograde flow/axoplasmic transport → stasis in the optic disc → extracellular edema (mechanical signs) and venous congestion (vascular signs). Acute: blurring of disc margins (earliest), elevated OD, Paton's lines (retinochoroidal folds around the OD d/t leakage of fluid); hyperemia/congestion of the OD, loss of venous pulsations, hemorrhages around the OD. Chronic: champagne-cork appearance. OD swollen → VFD: enlargement of the blind spot. ICP symptoms: papilledema (no LOV, normal light reflex, later 2° atrophy with gradual painless loss), horizontal diplopia (associated CN VI palsy), amaurosis fugax (brief cessation of axoplasmic transport; transient complete LOV, 30-60s episodes, total 6/6 recovery, diagnostic of stroke); headache (earliest sign, ↑ in morning, projectile vomiting, progressively worsens). Rx: depends on the underlying cause of ↑ ICP. Frisen's grading: 1 — 'C' shaped halo; 2 — circumferential halo, blurred margins; 3 — loss of major vessels around the disc; 4 — loss of vessels on the disc, ↑↑ swelling over disc; 5 — all vessels obscured, venous engorgement → congestion. AION: loss of blood supply to the anterior ON. Arteritic: giant cell arteritis (large vessel arteritis), temporal artery pathology, premonitory symptoms (pain, amaurosis fugax), B/L severe visual loss, corticosteroids. Non-arteritic (no vasculitis): occlusion of the short posterior ciliary artery; hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, collagen vascular diseases; painless, U/L moderate visual loss; experimental Rx levodopa + carbidopa × 3 weeks. Both: altitudinal field defects.
